name: Sandakpur
tagline: Four of the world's five highest peaks from one ridge top
meta_description: Sandakpur (Sandakphu), 3,636 m on the Nepal–India border: Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga in one view. Routes from Ilam, season, tips.
summary: Sandakpur, called Sandakphu in India, is the 3,636 m high point of the Singalila ridge on the Nepal–India border, north of Ilam. On a clear morning you see Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga, four of the five highest mountains on earth. From Nepal it is a long jeep day or a 3–5 day walk.
intro: The Singalila ridge runs south from the Kanchenjunga massif and forms the border between Nepal and India, 3,000 to 3,600 m high for much of its length. Sandakpur is its highest point. From the top the whole Kanchenjunga range fills the northern sky, about 65 km away, and on clear mornings Everest, Lhotse and Makalu stand to the west on the horizon. Few viewpoints anywhere put four of the five highest mountains on earth in a single sweep.

Most foreigners know the Indian side, the Singalila trek from Manebhanjyang near Darjeeling, with its old Land Rovers and trekkers' huts. Far fewer come up from Nepal. The Nepali approach starts from Ilam district, through Mai Pokhari and the ridge villages of Sandakpur rural municipality, by jeep on a rough road or on foot over several days. It is quieter, more rural and closer to village life than the Indian route.

The summit area straddles the border, and its lodges and huts are on the Indian side. On the Nepal side are smaller settlements and homestays, run by farming and herding families. We plan the trip so you are on the ridge for sunrise, with a night as close to the top as current rules and roads allow, and a spare morning in case cloud hides the view the first time.

story.title: The ridge between two countries
paras: The Singalila ridge lies between Limbuwan, the old Limbu homeland to the west, and Sikkim to the east. Herders have long brought cattle and yaks up to its high pastures in summer, and footpaths follow the crest rather than the steep river valleys below. The border between Nepal and Sikkim, and later India, was drawn along the watershed, which is why the frontier today follows the ridge almost exactly, marked by small pillars along the trail.

In the 20th century Sandakphu became famous from the Darjeeling side, where colonial-era walkers and later Indian trekkers came for the view of Kanchenjunga. The Indian side protected its forests as Singalila National Park, and a jeep road along the ridge brought a steady stream of visitors. On the Nepal side, the ridge stayed a farming and herding frontier, reached by footpaths from Ilam and visited mostly by local people, traders and pilgrims to Mai Pokhari below.

That is slowly changing. Since 2017 the ridge villages have formed Sandakpur rural municipality, named after the peak, and the municipality promotes the Nepal-side route with jeep tracks, homestays and viewpoints. Visitor numbers on the Nepal side remain small, and the walk through rhododendron and bamboo forest still feels like a farm trail more than a tourist route. Families who once lived only from cardamom, potatoes and cattle now host guests as well.

legend: People who live in the shadow of Kanchenjunga say its name means the five treasures of the high snow. In a belief held by the Lhopo of Sikkim and shared in stories on both sides of the ridge, the five summits hide treasures such as salt, gold and turquoise, sacred scriptures, armour, grain and medicine, which will be revealed to the devout when the world is in danger. From Sandakpur you look straight at those five summits.
people: The settlements along the Nepal side of the ridge are small and mixed: Sherpa and other families of Tibetan descent who herd yaks and run lodges higher up, and Limbu, Rai, Gurung, Tamang and Chhetri farming households lower down. Many grow cardamom, potatoes and vegetables, and keep cattle. Nepali is the common language. Families on both sides of the border are often related and cross freely.

untold.fact: Sandakphu, at 3,636 m, is the highest point of the Singalila ridge and also the highest point of the Indian state of West Bengal, while sitting on the border with Nepal.

Sandakpur rural municipality in Ilam district was created on 10 March 2017 in Nepal's restructuring of local government, and it includes the Mai Pokhari Ramsar wetland as well as the Sandakpur peak area.
The Singalila ridge, 3,000–3,500 m high south of Kanchenjunga, is the line that separates Sikkim in India from Nepal, which is why the border runs along the trail at Sandakpur.

taste.name: Chhurpi
taste.text: Hard, smoked cheese made from yak or cow milk, cut into small cubes and chewed for an hour or more. Herders and lodge owners on the ridge make and sell it. Buy a string from a lodge or in Ilam bazaar for the walk; it lasts for weeks.

highlights.title: Four eight-thousanders at sunrise
highlights.text: On clear mornings, Everest (8,849 m), Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) are visible from the top, four of the five highest mountains in the world. October to December gives the best chance of a clean view.

highlights.title: The full Kanchenjunga range
highlights.text: Kanchenjunga and its neighbours stretch across the northern horizon about 65 km away, with Jannu (Kumbhakarna) to its west. The long profile of the range is what most people come for, and it fills a wide-angle frame.

highlights.title: Rhododendron forest in April
highlights.text: The ridge forests are full of rhododendron, magnolia and bamboo. In April the gurans bloom red, pink and white along the trail, and the mornings are often clear enough for views before cloud rises from the valleys.

highlights.title: The Nepal-side approach
highlights.text: Few foreigners come up from Ilam. The Nepal-side route passes Mai Pokhari, farm villages and ridge forest, with homestays rather than trekkers' lodges, and very little traffic on the trail even in October.

highlights.title: Red panda country
highlights.text: The bamboo and rhododendron forests along the Singalila ridge are home to red pandas. Sightings are rare and need luck and patience, but the habitat is easy to see from the trail, especially in the quiet early hours.

how_to_reach.text: From Ilam bazaar, jeep tracks climb north through Mai Pokhari and the ridge villages toward the Sandakpur area, a long and rough day of roughly 6–8 hours. Sections are unpaved and can close in the monsoon. Check current status before you travel.
A walking route from the Ilam side takes 3–5 days up and down, staying in village homestays, with the last day on the forested ridge. We can combine jeep and walking to fit your time.
The nearest airport is Bhadrapur in Jhapa, about 45–50 minutes from Kathmandu. From there it is 3–4 hours to Ilam before the climb to the ridge.

where_to_stay: On the Nepal side, stays are village homestays and small family lodges along the ridge approach, with shared toilets, thick blankets and dal bhat cooked on a wood stove. The established lodges and huts at the summit itself sit on the Indian side of the border. Before and after the ridge, Ilam bazaar has simple hotels and guesthouses. We confirm current homestays and border arrangements before each trip.
tips: Aim for October to December for the clearest views; spring brings flowers but more haze and afternoon cloud.
At 3,636 m nights fall below freezing for much of the year, so bring a warm sleeping bag and down jacket.
Ascend gradually and drink plenty of water; mild altitude headaches are common on the first night above 3,000 m.
Foreign nationals other than Indians should not cross onto the Indian side of the ridge without the correct Indian visa and permits.
Carry cash in Nepali rupees and a power bank; there are no ATMs and electricity on the ridge can be limited.

experiences.title: Sunrise on Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga
experiences.summary: The reason to come: standing on the Singalila ridge before dawn as the light reaches Kanchenjunga, then Makalu, Lhotse and Everest far to the west. Four of the five highest peaks on earth in one sweep of the eye.
body: We wake you about an hour before sunrise and walk up in the dark to the best viewpoint near your night stop. It is cold, often well below freezing from November to March, and the wind can be sharp on the crest. Hot tea in a flask helps, and so does a down jacket, hat and gloves. Our guide picks a spot sheltered from the wind with a clear line both north to Kanchenjunga and west toward Everest.

Kanchenjunga lights first, its long massif filling the northern horizon in pink and then gold. Then the view swings west: Makalu's pyramid, Lhotse, and Everest standing slightly back, more than 100 km away. Our guide names the peaks and the smaller summits in between, including Jannu (Kumbhakarna) near Kanchenjunga, and points out the valleys of Nepal and Sikkim spread below, still filled with cloud and shadow while the snow is already lit.

Clouds usually rise from the valleys by mid-morning, so the hour after sunrise is the one that counts. If the first morning is cloudy, a spare night gives you a second chance, which is why we build one into most Sandakpur trips. Once the light is up, we walk back for breakfast, porridge, eggs or chapati with milk tea, and you can stay on the ridge or begin the walk or drive down.

faqs.q: Can you really see Everest from Sandakpur?
faqs.a: Yes. On clear mornings Everest, Lhotse and Makalu are visible to the west, and Kanchenjunga dominates the north. Everest is far away, so it looks smaller than Kanchenjunga. The best odds are October to December; in spring and summer cloud often hides the western peaks.

faqs.q: What camera lens is best at Sandakpur?
faqs.a: A wide lens for the whole Kanchenjunga range and a telephoto of 200 mm or more for Everest, Lhotse and Makalu, which are far away. Bring spare batteries in an inside pocket, as cold drains them fast before dawn, and a small tripod for the low light.

faqs.q: What if it is cloudy on the morning we are there?
faqs.a: It happens, especially in spring and the monsoon. We suggest a spare night on or near the ridge so you get two sunrise chances. Mornings are usually clearer than afternoons, so we plan your arrival for the afternoon before and keep the next morning flexible.

experiences.title: Walk to Sandakpur from the Ilam side
experiences.summary: A quiet multi-day walk from the Ilam side up to the Singalila ridge, through farm villages, cardamom plots and rhododendron forest, staying in family homestays and ending with sunrise on four of the world's five highest peaks at 3,636 m.
body: This is a farm-and-forest walk rather than a lodge trek. We drive from Ilam to the trailhead, usually near Mai Pokhari or a village beyond it, and walk on village paths through maize, cardamom and potato fields. Nights are in homestays where families cook dinner and you sleep in a spare room. You pass schools, small shops, water mills and shrines, and meet more farmers than trekkers.

Higher up the trail enters forest of rhododendron, oak, magnolia and bamboo, and the villages thin out to herders' huts and small clearings. The last day climbs onto the ridge itself, where the views open to the north. Daily walking is 4–6 hours with steady climbs; the route is moderate if you are fit and used to hills. Paths can be muddy and slippery after rain, and the last climb to the ridge is steep.

After sunrise on the ridge we walk or drive down, depending on the road, and return to Ilam for a hot shower and a proper bed. We arrange a licensed guide, porters if you want them and the homestays, and keep the pace slow enough to enjoy the villages. The route can be shortened by using a jeep for part of the way up or down, which suits travellers with less time.

faqs.q: How hard is the walk to Sandakpur from Nepal?
faqs.a: It is moderate: 4–6 hours a day on steep village paths and forest trails, climbing to 3,636 m. You need to be fit and comfortable with long uphill days. There are no technical sections. Rain makes the paths slippery, so good boots matter.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Sandakpur from the Nepal side?
faqs.a: The Nepal side of Sandakpur is not a national park or restricted area, so no special trekking permit has been needed as far as we know. Crossing onto the Indian side requires Indian entry papers. Rules can change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do we sleep on the Sandakpur walk?
faqs.a: In village homestays and small family lodges on the Nepal side. Rooms are simple, with shared toilets, blankets and home-cooked dal bhat. Bring a sleeping bag rated to about minus 10 °C for the ridge night, and a head torch, as electricity can be limited.

experiences.title: Rhododendron and red panda forest on the ridge
experiences.summary: A slow half-day walk through the high forest just below the ridge, with a guide who knows the birds and plants. In April the rhododendrons bloom; all year this bamboo and fir forest is red panda habitat.
body: Below the crest, the Singalila ridge is covered in mixed forest: rhododendron, oak, magnolia, silver fir and thick bamboo, hung with moss and lichen. It is one of the places in Nepal where the red panda lives, feeding on bamboo shoots and leaves and resting in tall trees. The forest is also home to barking deer, Himalayan black bears and many birds, though most animals keep well away from the trail.

We walk slowly in the early morning, when birds are active and the light is soft. Red panda sightings are rare and need luck; even so, you learn to read the habitat, from dense bamboo near water to the tall trees where the animals rest, and you may see laughingthrushes, sunbirds, pheasants and other ridge birds. In April the gurans flower red, pink and white along the path.

This walk fits easily into the day after sunrise, before the drive or walk down. We keep groups small and quiet, never use bait, and do not follow animals off the trail if we do see one. Our guide carries binoculars and a field guide, and helps with names of birds and plants. Bring a camera with a long lens and patience; the forest rewards those who stop and listen.

faqs.q: Will I see a red panda at Sandakpur?
faqs.a: Possibly, but do not count on it. Red pandas are shy, few in number and well camouflaged in the canopy. Early mornings in quiet forest give the best chance. We never use bait or chase animals, and we keep groups small and quiet.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom on the Singalila ridge?
faqs.a: Usually from late March to early May, peaking in April, with lower forests flowering first and higher ones on the ridge later. The exact timing shifts each year with the weather and snow, so we check with contacts in the ridge villages before your trip.

faqs.q: Is this walk suitable for older travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are already on the ridge. It is a slow walk of 2–3 hours on forest paths at about 3,000–3,600 m, with gentle ups and downs. Altitude makes everything feel harder, so we keep the pace easy and stop often.

experiences.title: Jeep to the ridge with a homestay night
experiences.summary: The short version for travellers with less time: a long jeep day from Ilam up to the ridge villages, a night in a homestay near the top, sunrise on the four great peaks, and the drive back down.
body: We leave Ilam early and drive north past Mai Pokhari, then on unpaved tracks up through ridge villages and forest. The drive is long, roughly 6–8 hours with stops, and bumpy in places, with steep sections where passengers sometimes walk while the jeep climbs. Our drivers know the road and the weather, and we stop for tea and lunch in the villages, with time to stretch and take photographs.

The night is in a homestay close to the ridge. Dinner is hot and simple, and the family keeps a fire going in the kitchen, the warmest room in the house. Conversation turns to cattle, potatoes, cardamom and the changes the jeep road has brought. Before dawn we walk up to the viewpoint for sunrise on Kanchenjunga, Makalu, Lhotse and Everest, with tea in a flask.

After breakfast we drive back to Ilam, arriving by late afternoon. Because the altitude gain is fast, from about 1,300 m to over 3,000 m in a day, we watch for headaches and keep a lower-altitude fallback plan. If anyone feels unwell, we sleep lower and go up for sunrise the next morning instead. A spare day in the plan makes the whole trip calmer.

faqs.q: Can I drive to Sandakpur from Ilam?
faqs.a: Jeep tracks now climb from the Ilam side toward the Sandakpur area, but the road is long, rough and partly unpaved, and can close in the monsoon. Only 4WD vehicles with local drivers should attempt it. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk at Sandakpur?
faqs.a: At 3,636 m, mild symptoms such as headache and poor sleep are common, especially when you drive up fast. Serious altitude sickness is less common at this height but possible. Drink water, avoid alcohol the first night and tell your guide if you feel unwell.

faqs.q: Is the Sandakpur jeep trip suitable for children?
faqs.a: Older children who cope well with long, bumpy drives usually enjoy it. The cold night and fast altitude gain are the main concerns. We advise against it for very young children and anyone with heart or lung conditions without medical advice.

faqs.q: Is Sandakpur in Nepal or India?
faqs.a: Both. Sandakpur, called Sandakphu in India, sits on the border along the Singalila ridge. The summit area and its lodges are on the Indian side, in West Bengal, while the slopes and villages to the west are in Sandakpur rural municipality, Ilam district, Nepal.

faqs.q: Which mountains can you see from Sandakpur?
faqs.a: On a clear day: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) and its range to the north, and Everest, Lhotse and Makalu to the west. That is four of the five highest mountains in the world. Smaller peaks such as Jannu (Kumbhakarna) are also visible near Kanchenjunga.

faqs.q: How do I reach Sandakpur from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly to Bhadrapur (about 45–50 minutes), drive 3–4 hours to Ilam, then either take a long jeep day north to the ridge or walk 3–5 days from the Ilam side. Allow at least 5–6 days from Kathmandu and back. Check current status of roads before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Sandakpur?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest mountain views. March and April bring rhododendron flowers with more haze and afternoon cloud. January and February are clear but very cold, with possible snow. June to September is monsoon, with cloud, rain and leeches.

faqs.q: How cold is Sandakpur?
faqs.a: Nights at 3,636 m drop below freezing for much of the year and well below in December to February, with possible snow. Days can be pleasant in sun. Bring a down jacket, warm sleeping bag, hat and gloves in all seasons except high summer.

faqs.q: Can foreigners cross to the Indian side at Sandakpur?
faqs.a: Nepali and Indian citizens cross the ridge freely. Other nationals need a valid Indian visa and the permits required for Singalila National Park, and there is no formal immigration post on the ridge. We plan Nepal-side routes for foreign travellers. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Nepal-side Sandakpur trek crowded?
faqs.a: No. Most trekkers use the Indian route from Manebhanjyang. On the Nepal side from Ilam you mostly meet farmers, herders and the occasional group of Nepali visitors, especially in autumn. Holidays such as Dashain bring more domestic visitors, but the trail is still quiet by Nepal standards.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for Sandakpur?
faqs.a: We strongly recommend a licensed local guide. The Nepal-side paths are not well signed, homestays need arranging, the border runs along the ridge, and weather changes fast. A guide also makes the village stays far richer, translating and explaining what you see.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Sandakpur?
faqs.a: From Ilam: two days by jeep with one night near the top, or 3–5 days on foot. Add a spare night for weather. Including travel from Kathmandu, plan 6–8 days for a relaxed trip with time in Ilam's tea gardens.
